title: Why Singapore Sprint weekend is such a challenge for drivers
excerpt:
Like any street race venue, Singapore has always been a big test for Formula 1 drivers as they build up their speed and confidence over the weekend in the run-up to Qualifying.

And as a night race, there is always the extra challenge of not just the normal ramping up of grip that you get on any street track, but also the change in conditions associated with the move from daylight to darkness sessions.

Throw in the heat and punishing night race schedule, with its early morning finishes for drivers and team members, and Singapore is one of the toughest events on the schedule.

This year the Sprint format has added a further dimension. Everyone has just the Friday FP1 session with which to get their eye in before plunging into Sprint Qualifying – thus they will have to get up to limit a lot earlier than they usually do at a street venue, which inevitably creates some risk.

Add in the fact that the single practice session will be held in the daytime, Sprint Qualifying that follows is at night, and then the Sprint itself is set to take place in sunshine, and it won’t be easy for anyone to hit the set-up sweet spot that is ideal for all circumstances.

“It’s going to be very interesting,” says World Championship leader Kimi Antonelli. “First of all, a Sprint weekend in a city circuit is always very challenging, because the track just evolves so quickly that it's going to be so different from session to session.

“Also, FP1 tomorrow is going to be in the day, and Quali is going to be in the night. So it's going to be very, very different. But it's a good challenge for us drivers, for the team.”

Coping with changing grip conditions will be the key, and Max Verstappen believes it is important to start from a good baseline in practice.

“As every year here, you know that during the day you have a little bit less grip,” says the Sepang winner. “It's probably a little bit harder on the tyres. But the most important thing is just to find a good balance with the car straight away in FP1. That will probably just help a lot for the rest of your weekend.

“It's always hectic, a Sprint weekend, to make the right choices. And sometimes you just have a better one, or you have a bit more of a more straightforward one than others. But at the moment, it's very difficult to know how it's going to go.

“But yeah, naturally, when you drive during the day at a Sprint compared to in the night, it will have different challenges. But at the same time, we also know that this track is very hard to pass.

“So I think at the end of the day, the most important thing is qualifying for Sprint, or the race, because that normally defines where you finish.”

Just as some drivers take more time to get up to speed, some teams have a better record of arriving with a car suited to a given track. Lewis Hamilton is confident that Ferrari fall into that category and can thus count on being strong from FP1 onwards.

“I honestly think we generally hit the ground often running pretty well, more often than not, in FP1,” says the seven-time World Champion. “And then from session to session, some people close up, some people pull away. But I think our simulation team did a really great job, and more often than not, the car started in a not a terrible place throughout the year.

“So I'm hoping that we start from the right place, and it's exciting to come here, to come to Singapore, and you only have one session. Everyone's in the same boat, so it could be good, could be not good. But we'll see how it goes tomorrow.”

Russell promises 'all-out attack' in Singapore amid penalty

Alex Albon echoes the theme of starting with a solid set-up, and he makes an interesting observation about the day/night changes.

“It’s not so much the temperature, but it's what the sun does to the tyres as it comes out and goes down,” says the Williams driver. “So what you'll see normally in FP1 and FP3, the tyres are quite easy to get up to temperature and get them to work. And as soon as the sun drops, the tyres take on a completely different response. But we're used to that because that's been here every year.

“In terms of set-up changes, you kind of go into this weekend with a little bit more of a baseline, something that kind of we know will work, something that that fits most tracks.

“Most probably, you go on the side of confidence, whether that's through ride, suspension, just general set-up being a little bit more understeer, and then you kind of try to build the weekend a little bit differently like that.”

The schedule is the same for everyone, but it will be an especially tough test for Arvid Lindblad as the only rookie in the field.

The Briton has had to learn other tracks on Sprint weekends already this season, but he agrees that Singapore will be particularly tricky.

“It's just a normal tendency of the night races that you do have some sessions a little bit more in the daylight,” says the Racing Bulls driver. “So you don't have that similarity across the five sessions, let's say. Yes, that's an added challenge.

“I would say that maybe I can relate a bit more to F2. I'd have to have a look to the last year to have a look at how much the lap times improved.

"It was very often in F2 when we’d do a practice during the day on the hard [tyre], and then you’d go to Qualifying at night on the soft, and you go like five seconds quicker.

“I don't think it'll be that much here, but I've had it where you go back out and you have a load more grip, and you have to just get on it.”

That building up of confidence on a wall-lined track will be harder for Lindblad than anyone else, given that thus far he has only seen it in the simulator.

“You still can build up, but it's obviously a very different way you have to do that,” he says. “I experienced that in Canada. I really tried to make an effort in the first run to just build up the confidence and get comfortable, and then you start to push on towards the last laps of FP1, and then more in Sprint Quali.

“It's true that it's not easy because on street circuits, it is all about building up. In the end, all that matters is that you go into Qualifying confident and comfortable.

“And I didn't do the best job of that in the previous two street circuits; I crashed twice in FP2. But obviously I can learn from that, and it was a valuable lesson. But it's even harder now on a Sprint weekend, because you have even fewer sessions. So it's something I'm thinking about – how to get that balance right.”

title: All the stories that got the Singapore paddock talking
excerpt:
The Singapore Grand Prix has seen six different winners in the last six years – and remarkably one of those winners is not Max Verstappen. However, the four-time World Champion is being tipped as the favourite for victory by many as the paddock reconvened under the lights at Marina Bay...

Verstappen cautious about chances of victory

Given his victory in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was his first of the season, extending his run of winning at least one race a season to 11 years, it's perhaps understandable that Verstappen didn't want to get carried away with his chances of making it back-to-back victories.

title: Why splitting car specs is a 'no-brainer' for Mercedes
excerpt:
Mercedes have committed to an unusual strategy for the Singapore Grand Prix, as it will field its two W17s with completely different aero packages over what will already be a hectic and complicated Sprint weekend.

While Kimi Antonelli will stick with the updates as seen in Sepang last weekend, George Russell will revert to the previous version, thus giving the team a direct back-to-back comparison over all three days of the event.

Mercedes have taken this approach because the results produced by the new updates, which were introduced in Malaysia, proved to be inconclusive.

It was hardly a disaster, given that Antonelli finished second and Russell was destined for the podium before his late retirement, but the feeling in the camp was that it didn’t produce the lap time benefits anticipated.

Russell floated the idea of using Singapore as a back-to-back test even before the Sepang race, but his retirement guaranteed him a power unit grid penalty for this weekend, making the decision an obvious one.

“I instigated the conversation prior to the race on Sunday,” he said on Thursday's media day in Singapore. “So when the failure happened, it was kind of a no-brainer, because we were kind of 50-50 about it pre-race. And I was more in favour to do it, and that was even pre-race. Whereas now it is a total no-brainer.”

Russell may well find out that he has drawn the short straw, but it’s a risk that he is willing to take and he sees a bigger picture of helping the team to draw firm conclusions about the new parts.

“I think for any team, it's always very important,” he said. “However, there's no signs telling us the upgrade was not working, and we know the car we had in Baku was the same car as we had in Budapest and Zandvoort, and in Baku we were on pole by eight-tenths, and in Budapest, we were four-tenths off the pace.

“So those fluctuations, even with a consistent car and your rivals with the same car, are drastic. You have a fluctuation plus or minus one second, it can be, that delta. So we're pretty confident it's Malaysia specific.

“When you look at the pace of Red Bull as well, they clearly over performed compared to where they've been this season compared to all of the other teams, and actually, when you look at our pace compared to McLaren and Ferrari, it wasn't too dissimilar. It wasn't like massively out of bed.

“So this engine penalty this weekend has just given a good opportunity to roll back. It's the car that I won in Baku with – so let's see.”

Russell promises 'all-out attack' in Singapore amid penalty

In addition to the parts seen in Sepang, Antonelli also has a new front wing in Singapore, which in effect completes the update package but it remains to be seen whether or not that’s the key that makes it come alive.

The Italian acknowledges that last weekend the updates didn’t produce the expected gains in Malaysia.

“Of course, the numbers are a different story in Sepang,” said the Italian. “But I think Sepang, it was a bit of an outlier because the tarmac was just so rough. Actually, in some corners we were missing tarmac, and also it was so hot. We had at times 60-plus degree track temperatures, so I think was a bit of an outlier.

“And definitely I feel like this weekend is going to be a bit more representative. Cooler temperatures, the tarmac is in a much better state, and I think it's going to be a very good test, because in Sepang we struggled a lot in low-speed, and here we have a lot of low-speed.

“So let's see how it's going to be. And plus, we'll have two different cars on two different packages. So that is going to be interesting to see, we're going to have a straight comparison on that side.”

Antonelli has no qualms about sticking with the updates, and believes Singapore will get the best out of them.

“Well, I didn't really get to decide,” he said. “It was it was mainly the team that decided to go back on the old package. As I said before, we think it was it was an outlier, and we do believe the new package can work well. It's just a matter of trying to put the car in the right window, and understand it more.

“And this weekend, I think, is a good example. It's going to be a good opportunity to see and to compare the two packages. And because we know the old one, we've known it for ages, we know how to set up the car around that package. We know it works really well, and is really fast in these kinds of tracks. And we really want to understand.

“On the other hand, this new package and trying to really strike the maximum out of it, because the team has done a tremendous job. They've put in so much work on this new package, and it would be just a shame to write it off so early.

“So I feel like I'm quite comfortable on keeping it – and actually I really want to help the team out to understand it more, and as I said before try to extract the potential.”

title: Ferrari drivers 'here to attack' in Singapore GP
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton insists that he and Ferrari team mate Charles Leclerc are "here to attack" during the Singapore Grand Prix this weekend.

Hamilton arrives after a fightback drive last time out in Malaysia, where the wrong tyre strategy initially on a wet track meant the seven-time World Champion had to claw his way back to the podium from towards the rear of the field.

It was the first podium for Hamilton since the British Grand Prix back in July, with the Briton insisting on Thursday's media day in Singapore that the result last weekend did not necessarily mean Ferrari were back in contention for victory.

"It's not that we come here with momentum, we've had one good race last weekend and we'll try and build on that," said Hamilton.

"I think this should be an okay circuit for us, there's lots of challenges, particularly that it's a Sprint weekend, which makes this track the most challenging of the year. We're just going over the numbers and trying to make sure we start in the right place."

He added: "I've been pushing the car in a certain direction and I think we are slowly making gains and improvements. We're here to attack, Qualifying is key and it would be really great if we could start tomorrow on the right foot and then just attacking in Qualifying."

Despite a poor run of form over the last few events, Hamilton was hopeful that Ferrari's 2026 challenger would be better suited to Singapore's street venue, where a high downforce setup would be required.

"I think with our car it's generally good on street circuits, particularly when there's not long straights. If you look at the last races we're quick through corners, not so quick in a straight line," he said.

"This is a high drag circuit, so I'm hoping that the advantage others have on those long straights comes down a little bit and we can start matching them through corners."

Team mate Leclerc was cautious, however, believing that Ferrari may have slipped down in the performance pecking order, with the team's place as Mercedes' nearest opposition having been taken by McLaren and Red Bull in recent races.

"Historically we've been quite strong here, but we cannot really rely on the past," said Leclerc.

"We've got to do everything we can in order to be in the best possible situation. It's also true that the tendency lately has been that we're losing a bit of performance compared to the guys in front, so to win will be very difficult."

title: Verstappen evaluates chances of long-awaited Singapore win
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has insisted that he’s “going to try” to secure his first win at the Singapore Grand Prix, but remains aware that even after his victory in Malaysia, “there are no guarantees” due to the tight competition at the front of the field.

Following a frustrating start to the 2026 season, Verstappen finally returned to the top step last time out at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, where he beat Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli and Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton.

Although the achievement suggested that Red Bull might be able to fight for wins regularly, the Dutchman explained that it would be “complicated” to do so at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, especially as his best result there was a trio of P2 finishes in 2025, 2024 and 2018.

Quizzed on whether he’s now in a place to chase down that long-awaited win in Singapore, he replied: “We're going to try, that's for sure. It's always complicated on a street circuit, a lot of things have to come together.

“Some just happen a bit sooner than others and unfortunately for a lot of different reasons, we have not won here yet, even in our dominant years.

“But you always need to look at the strengths of the car and Singapore was a track where our car didn't really come alive before. I hope it's going to be a little bit better this year but there are no guarantees.

“There are a lot of other teams that are also very strong on street circuits and also every street circuit is very different. This is not like Baku, for example, and it's also not like Monaco. We'll see.”

With seven rounds of the season remaining, Verstappen went on to explain that he wants to stay realistic about Red Bull’s chances and set just one goal – to seal another win before they shift their focus to 2027.

“I just want to try and see if we can carry this momentum and try to be in a position again to win potentially,” he said. “I don't know if that's here or in another race.

“We have won one race finally and then we also need to stay with two feet on the ground and keep working because I'm sure that it's not always going to be like this now until the end of the season. Step by step we try to be better and next year is a completely different story.”

Verstappen’s triumph in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia would’ve been made even sweeter by a double podium for the team, and while Isack Hadjar came close, a battery issue dropped him to P5 late on.

Reflecting on the weekend, Hadjar said: “To be honest, it's still an ongoing analysis, but at the same time, I don't think whatever happened in Malaysia is going to impact us heading into Singapore.

“But still, I'm not the type of guy who just moves on anyway, ‘ah, the race is finished’. I want everything to be understood and, even if now I'm focused on Singapore, I am happy to then come back into a bit more details.”

It was nevertheless a strong showing by the Frenchman, who was able to celebrate a historic first win for Red Bull Ford Powertrains just two races into his return from injury.

“[When] we started in Melbourne, I was like nine-tenths behind Mercedes in third. And then we kind of went downhill, so at some point we were even further away from the leaders, and from then we kind of managed to reach decent results, had some form, average form.

“I would say it was kind of a plateau for a bit of the European period, and then that final upgrade kind of put us in contention, and also you have Max in the car so it kind of helps. It's great to have a Red Bull power unit win a race. They've been doing that for only four years and they won an F1 race already, so it's impressive.”

title: Mercedes will 'find an answer' to unlocking upgrades – Antonelli
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli believes that Mercedes can “find an answer” as to why their most recent upgrades haven’t delivered the intended performance boost, with the Italian set to run a new front wing designed to complement the package in Singapore.

While rival teams such as Ferrari and Red Bull introduced fairly regular updates over the season, Mercedes opted to wait until the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia to make major changes to their challenger, including altered bodywork and adjustments to the floor.

They had hoped that these would reinstate the performance advantage they enjoyed earlier in the season, but that didn’t quite come to fruition. Instead, Red Bull’s Max Verstappen converted pole position into a win for the first time in 2026, while George Russell retired due to a mechanical issue.

Although Antonelli still finished on the podium behind Verstappen, the race showed that Mercedes have work to do in order to optimise their current package over the remaining rounds.

Asked whether a new front wing will help the upgrades to perform as they should, Antonelli responded: “That's the question we will try to answer. George is going back on the old package, which we know works really well, especially on these kinds of tracks.

“On my side, we'll try to find an answer for this package. Hopefully we will understand it more and finally strike the potential of the package. Of course we'll have the front wing, even though it's just one front wing, but let's see.

“I think Sepang overall was a little bit of an outlier because of the tarmac, the high temperatures, but hopefully this weekend we will be able to put the car in a better place and just extract more out of the package.”

Alongside reverting to a previous specification, Russell will also receive a significant grid penalty for exceeding his power unit allocation, giving Antonelli an opportunity to further increase his advantage in the drivers’ standings.

He currently leads his team mate by 84 points, but insisted that his attention remains on working to get the most out of Mercedes’ upgrades rather than thinking about the ongoing battle against Russell.

“I've committed with the new package and I will commit for the whole weekend,” he said. “There's no way to go back to it because it's a big job for the team.

“We will try to do the best with what we have but I'm more confident coming to this weekend because I feel like hopefully we will have a better understanding of the package and we will be able to extract more of its potential.

“We're going to try and win. That's the mindset and of course, George is starting at the back but it doesn't mean anything. On my side I just try to focus on what I can control and try to deliver the best performance as I can and if I can win the race, great.

“If I have to do a podium, I will do a podium. I'm really looking forward to the weekend and hopefully we can achieve a great result with the team.”

title: Russell promises ‘all-out attack’ in Singapore amid penalty
excerpt:
George Russell has promised an “all-out attack” in the Singapore Grand Prix as he prepares to line up at the back of the grid thanks to an engine-related penalty.

Russell has been forced to take on new power unit components following his late-race retirement at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last time out, which cost him valuable championship points.

The subsequent penalty will be a minimum of 10 positions depending on the exact parts Mercedes switch out, and how many of his allowances for the season that he exceeds.

As per the regulations, the first time the allocation of any one of the elements is exceeded, a 10-place grid penalty will be applied, with the second time this occurs (and so on) resulting in a five-place grid drop – all penalties at the same event applying in a cumulative manner.

If a driver incurs a penalty exceeding 15 grid places, they will be required to start the race at the back of the field regardless.

Asked about his mindset and approach arriving in Singapore, with the grid penalty hanging over him, Russell said: “All-out attack; just trying to enjoy the weekend.

“Obviously, if you could choose where to take the penalty in the season, this [track] would be probably the second bottom of the list after Monaco. But unfortunately, just with how things have panned out, we have no choice but to take it here.

“Also, because it’s so early, we’ve still got seven races to go, we’ll probably have to take another one down the line as well, so it’s obviously not an ideal situation. But Singapore is a place I love, and I’ll try and carve my way through the pack.”

Another topic of note for Mercedes heading into the Marina Bay event is the team’s plan to run old and new versions of their W17 challenger – championship leader Kimi Antonelli due to press on with the latest updates, and Russell set to revert to the package he drove to pole position and victory in Azerbaijan.

“It is back,” said Russell of his previous specification car, given the question marks over Mercedes’ upgrades at Sepang. “Obviously Malaysia was the worst weekend of the year for us as a team, in terms of pace, Qualifying result.

“Of course, we probably both would have been on the podium, but it was a difficult one, and we don’t know whether that was Malaysia specific or whether that was anything to do with the upgrade.

“There are no major signs telling us it’s anything to do with the upgrade, but we don’t measure performance in F1 on how much downforce a car produces. You measure it with a stopwatch, and the stopwatch wasn’t great in Malaysia, so let’s see this weekend.

“I’m very happy to be back on that package and do the compare, and I’m not really in any sort of fight this weekend, or the championship for that regard, so it’s the right place to do it.”

Russell’s penalty will be applied for Sunday’s Singapore Grand Prix, rather than Saturday’s Sprint, in which eight points are up for grabs.

title: Norris ‘hopeful’ recent car issue will be cured in Singapore
excerpt:
Lando Norris has offered an honest assessment of McLaren’s last two race weekends, stating that he and the team have “underperformed” and “need to do a better job” moving forward.

Boosted by mid-season updates, Norris charged to three out of four pole positions, and two race victories, across the Budapest, Zandvoort, Monza and Madrid rounds – raising McLaren’s hopes for the final phase of the campaign.

However, the last two events at Baku and Sepang served as a reality check for the Woking-based team, with neither Norris nor team mate Oscar Piastri making it onto the podium, and the Briton being plagued by unspecified straight-line speed issues.

At the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Red Bull, Mercedes and Ferrari all appeared to have superior raw pace, leaving McLaren to scratch their heads and come up with some answers ahead of this weekend’s visit to Singapore.

Asked about the learnings from Sepang during Thursday’s media activities at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, Norris said: “Oh, there were a fair few, both from my side, and from us as a team. Obviously from what happened in the race, but also just general things from a car point of view and what we need to do a better job in, and how can we get back to the same level as we were in the previous few: Budapest, Zandvoort and Madrid.

“So, the team have been working very hard, we’ve all worked very hard to understand what we could learn from last weekend, what we can and need to do better in. The exact things, the specifics of it, I don’t need to go into, but there was a good amount.

“There were some obvious ones, such as the straight-line speed, and the issues I’ve been having with the car, and obviously more technical ones, [like] how can we unlock more potential from the car to get back to the performance that we had previously. That’s a tricky one to do.”

As for whether some of McLaren’s deficit at Sepang was track-specific, Norris continued: “Well, at Baku we weren’t necessarily too quick either, so I wouldn’t say just a Malaysia thing. There are certainly some aspects of Malaysia, with the roughness of the tarmac, that we think does play a part.

“It’s a good thing for us to see this weekend if some of the performance that we were missing there does come back. Singapore is a track I’ve enjoyed, and we’ve been pretty good here over the last few years.

“Certainly, a little bit of it is track layout, and the last couple of tracks have not been to the same strengths as what we’ve seen in Madrid and some of the other races, but all in all we’ve still been underperforming to the level we need to and we want to be, so we still need to do a better job no matter what.”

Norris was then asked about the work McLaren have been carrying out in a bid to get on top of the specific straight-line speed issue he has been facing over the last couple of events, with the Briton “hopeful” things will be back to normal this time out.

“We need to get it on track first and see how much better [it is],” added Norris, who claimed pole and the race win in Singapore in 2024, as well as podium finishes in 2023 and 2025. “It’s obviously also a circuit where straight lines are not like the highest priority, and not as detrimental as the last few weekends.

“Nevertheless, you always want to go down the straights as quickly as what you should be able to. It’s always tough when you come out of corners better and end up going slower. It’s been a frustrating two weekends trying to figure out what the issue has been and why there’s just been a constant lack of straight-line speed and performance.

“Especially in this kind of battle we’ve been in [at the front of the grid], the last two Qualifyings it’s been [a difference of] two or three positions, so it’s cost me quite a lot. At the same time, there’s obviously things I can do better as well.

“I’m confident that the team have done a good job. They’ve put a lot of work into trying to figure out things. I’m hopeful that it will be better this weekend, but honestly I have to get out on track and see first.”

McLaren head into the Singapore weekend holding third position in the Teams’ Championship standings on 316 points, behind Ferrari on 405 and leaders Mercedes on 556, and just 18 points ahead of fourth-placed Red Bull.

title: Verstappen answers your questions in our exclusive Q&A
excerpt:
This weekend, Max Verstappen will celebrate his 250th Grand Prix on the streets of Singapore, bringing another milestone in the Dutchman’s trophy-filled F1 career that began just over a decade ago.

To mark the special occasion, F1.com recently sat down with the four-time World Champion and put your questions to him – topics spanning his F1 journey, off-track interests, future goals and much more.

So, without further ado, read on (or watch) below to find out if your question made it into Verstappen’s bag of fan mail, and what he said in response…

Emma, UK: What is the best advice someone ever gave you that helped you in many areas of your life?

Just be yourself! Stay with two feet on the ground. I think that’s the most important.

Andy, Canada: The 2024 Sao Paulo race was the gutsiest thing I have seen with you racing in the rain. What was going through your mind with almost zero visibility at those speeds? My teeth hurt from clenching when I watched it. Best race I have ever seen…

Well, I mean, I had another race in Sao Paulo in 2016 that was probably… I would say even worse in terms of visibility at times. But yeah, it’s just… You’ve practiced a lot in your life driving in the wet in general, like racing in the rain. Yeah, the visibility at times is not great, but it’s the same for everyone, so you just have to deal with it. But for sure it was an insane race, and for me at the time, of course, a very important one to win.

Alexandra, Ukraine: Which F1 driver would you trust the most to babysit your cats?

Probably Alex Albon, because he has cats himself, like quite a few, so he definitely knows what to do!

Evan, Norway: What’s a hobby you've picked up that surprised you?

Well, I started playing padel like a few years ago now. I never really played any kind of racket sport before, so I didn’t know that that was on the horizon, but I enjoy it a lot.

Nancy, Canada: What is the best part of being a new dad?

The best part… I mean, just spending time with her and seeing her grow, seeing that it’s your little girl. That’s definitely the best part of it.

Nia Anand, Singapore: If all the F1 drivers on the grid were stuck in an airport overnight, who would solve the problem? Who would make it worse? And where would you be?

Well, who would solve the problem… I would solve the problem! Who would it make it worse? Who would make it worse, my God… Let’s just not get stuck in the airport, probably. I don’t know. I have no idea who would actually make it worse, because when you’re stuck in an airport that’s already, I guess, ‘worse’ enough. I don’t know what can be worse. If you’re stuck in an airport, what can you make worse? And where would I be? Where would I be? Well, stuck at the airport!

Robert, UK: If you were not racing in any form of motorsport, what would you be doing for a job?

I would still, I think, work in motorsport, but probably more in like a manager role or trying to just advise young talents – if I wouldn’t have succeeded in F1.

Lia, Ukraine: Looking back on your first 249 Grands Prix, which race taught you the biggest lesson?

It’s hard to pinpoint. I mean, to pick out one specific race, it’s just… Life, I guess, is a lesson, your career as well, your races, good and bad. You learn from every single race, some a little bit more than others. I think it’s just taking the general experience, and that probably makes you a better driver. It’s hard to just pick one particular race.

Cian, Ireland: If F1 had two-seater cars, who are you bringing into the cockpit and why?

Probably family members, friends… close friends and family members. I would not just take one person.

Verena, the Netherlands: What are some important values you have and live by, that help you be as successful as you are in F1 and in life?

Trying to live it as relaxed as possible, not really caring too much about stuff, social media… Just live your life normally, happy, with the people that you want to live it with. Try to keep it just very simple: keep life very simple.

Jaquavius, Brazil: What is your favourite food?

Good name! Tomato soup and beef carpaccio.

Ava, Australia: Which driver has challenged you the most in your career, on and off the track?

Which driver? It’s hard. It’s hard to pick one. I mean, in F1, of course, you have a lot of great drivers. I had a lot great team mates in go-karting. You learn from all of your team mates, for example, over your career… different things. I think it’s just the general experience of having your team mates challenge you, other drivers challenge you. It’s hard to just pick one particular person, I would say.

Prathik, India: Do you miss being Daniel Ricciardo’s team mate?

Yeah, well, I miss my times with Daniel, for sure. He’s a great guy. Sometimes we still catch up a little bit. Yeah, looking back at it, it was definitely a really fun period of my career also, with him. It’s definitely… When we see each other, we talk about it and have a good laugh.

Mina, Slovenia: What’s your favourite way to relax after a race weekend?

My favourite way to relax is probably just going home and spending time with my family, with the kids, just not thinking about racing too much.

Ibrahim, Australia: Have you ever lost hope at a certain point in your career? And if you have, how did you handle it?

No, I’ve not lost hope. I mean, you just need to keep trying to work towards your goal, and it’s not always an upwards trend or like a straight line. If you’re very passionate about what you do, and you love what you’re doing, you just keep going at it, and some days are better than others.

Alice, Czech Republic: What do you want your legacy to be?

Uhm, what do I want my legacy to be? As long as, I think, people can remember me as just being honest, straightforward, and always being myself, not trying to act like a different person suddenly… For me, that’s the most important, just to be remembered exactly like I am.

Joseph, USA: If you could have dinner with any F1 legend to discuss the sport or life, who would it be?

I never really had those kind of things [wishes]. I don’t want to meet anyone famous. I just want to spend time with my friends and family when I can, and that will be the best dinner anyway! Just with the people that you love, you have a great time, you laugh a lot, so I never really had the urge or desire to have dinner with someone that I don’t know.

Dana, Belgium: If you could say something to your little ‘you’ (when you were a child), what would you say?

I would say nothing. I would just let him live his life, experience the good things, the bad things, because at the end of the day, it all helps you to become a better driver, a better person. If you know everything in advance, probably life is very boring...

Maka Penny, Peru: Outside of the racing world, what’s something you still hope to achieve or build in your lifetime?

Travel the world more, spend time with my family and friends. It’s not really about achieving or building, it’s actually spending time with the people that you miss a lot throughout your F1 career.

Arek, Poland: If you could freely choose (from both current and past) one track, one car and one opponent to race against, what and who would you pick?

Spa, early 2000s F1 cars, maybe like 2004, and my dad.

Azra, Cyprus: What was your childhood nickname, if you had any?

I didn’t have any, because my name is nice and short! Max is very easy.

title: Kimi Antonelli reveals 'heat stroke' deterrent to using F1 safety device
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli has confirmed that two bad experiences last year have deterred him from using the cooling vest for this weekend's race in Singapore, where a heat hazard has been declared for the fourth time this season.

Ahead of the race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, Antonelli has confirmed that he suffered "a heat stroke" at the end of sprint qualifying for the 2025 United States Grand Prix in Austin due to a water pump failure that led to hot water being distributed.

The vest remains a divided subject amongst the drivers, with some believing it to be beneficial, whilst others like Antonelli feel it to be a nuisance.

Asked for his thoughts on the vest, and which side of the fence he was on, the championship-leading Mercedes driver said: "I don't worry because when I worried last year, I had two very bad experiences.

"The first time it didn't work for as long as we had hoped, and the second time, the pump system failed. I did the whole session with the system pumping the water at 50 degrees, so I suffered a heat stroke after the session. It wasn't very pleasant.

"Ever since, I've been like, I'm going to train hard, so I don't have to use it for the weekends."

[Article continues below]

Antonelli seeking assurances

Antonelli has not ruled out the prospect of using the vest in the future, provided it works properly.

"If we get to a point where it's developed, and we have the confidence that it's going to work every time, and for the time that we need it, I think it's very nice because it definitely keeps you cool," he said.

"But now there's so much uncertainty, that we're not so sure. Imagine on Sunday, you put it on, and after 30 minutes, it doesn't work anymore, and hot water is even worse.

"So on that side, I just want to be sure it's going to be fine, and that it's going to be well developed. When we have the confidence, then maybe I will put it [back on], but right now I will just train to be ready for any conditions."

title: Max Verstappen eyes Singapore 'extreme' as Red Bull prepare for latest test
excerpt:
Max Verstappen has never won the Singapore GP, doing so this weekend would perhaps represent Red Bull's biggest 2026 milestone yet.

Max Verstappen has stressed the need to nail his car's balance in Friday's only practice session at the Singapore Grand Prix, with Red Bull facing what the Dutchman has described as an "extreme" test of its recent upgrades on the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

Verstappen, who arrives in Singapore off the back of finishing second in Baku and winning in Sepang, is wary of the unique demands of a circuit long regarded as one of the toughest on the calendar, particularly given this weekend's Sprint format which adds another layer of complexity to Red Bull's preparation.

The Singapore GP is another wildly different venue to most on the calendar, with Azerbaijan and Malaysia having already offered Red Bull two unique tests.

In both, three practice sessions were at least on offer to understand the circuits and complete several different run plans, something which will be impossible in Singapore due to the sprint format.

Speaking to select media, including RacingNews365, the four-time world champion explained why getting on top of the car in FP1 will be crucial.

"As every year here, you know that during the day you have a little bit less grip," began Verstappen. "It's probably a little bit harder on the tyres, but the most important thing is just to find a good balance with the car straight away in FP1.

"That will probably just help a lot for the rest of your weekend. It's always hectic on a Sprint weekend to make the right choices, and sometimes you just have a better one, or you have a bit more of a straightforward one than others.

"At the moment, it's very difficult to know how it's going to go. Naturally, when you drive during the day in the sprint compared to at night, it will have different challenges. But at the same time, we also know that this track is very hard to pass. :

"So I think at the end of the day, the most important thing is qualifying for the sprint or the race because that normally defines where you finish."

Driver

Max Verstappen

3

Max Verstappen managing expectations in Red Bull bogey venue

Red Bull brought a revised floor and sidepod package to Baku last time out, aimed at sharpening the car's underbody performance.

But Verstappen made clear that Singapore represents a far tougher proving ground than either of Red Bull's two most recent outings.

Marina Bay has historically been a difficult venue for Red Bull. The bumps and high kerbs around the circuit tend to force ground-effect cars like Red Bull's above their optimal ride height window, eroding the aerodynamic performance that makes the car so strong elsewhere.

The stiffer mechanical setup the team typically favours to keep the platform stable can also struggle to absorb kerb strikes on Marina Bay's uneven surface, while the circuit's steady diet of short, low-speed 90-degree corners denies Red Bull the chance to exploit the high-speed efficiency and underfloor loading that normally play to its strengths.

Those characteristics help explain why Verstappen's two most recent Singapore outings, in 2024 and 2025, both ended in second place behind a rival.

Asked if there was any concern that the updates might not translate to Marina Bay, Verstappen replied: "The updates, they will work, sometimes some tracks are just naturally a little bit better for us.

"Baku, again, it's, colder, harder to switch on the tyres. Malaysia is, of course, the complete opposite, and this is again, of course, a hot place where the tyres do switch on, but we have had our limitations, so yeah, it's again, for me, another extreme compared to what we had in Baku or Malaysia.

"But I also know that some other cars are very good in low speed or specifically on street circuits. But we want to just try and be competitive and be in the hunt for the podium."

title: Lewis Hamilton airs unusual 'Whoop' fear in unique F1 challenge
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton has conceded that he is "really worried" about his sleep score over the Singapore Grand Prix weekend.

Formula 1 teams and drivers traditionally stay on European time throughout, a concession to the race's night-time slot under the Marina Bay Street Circuit's floodlights.

That means not going to bed until the early hours of the local morning, and sleeping through the daylight hours behind blackout blinds, a routine Hamilton says is playing havoc with his wearable 'Whoop' sleep tracker.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, the seven-time champion explained the toll the schedule is taking on his recovery data.

Asked about the different routine required in Singapore, Hamilton said: "I don't mind it. I don't like it or dislike it. It's a challenge, something different.

"My Whoop page is definitely going to be affected by this week, so I'm not too happy about that because my sleep score is down because I'm going to bed at three or four a.m.

"Even if I sleep and I feel like I have slept well, my sleep score is coming out like 40 per cent, and I'm really worried. So someday my sleep score is not going to be great.

"So that's something I'm thinking of every day, trying to get a good sleep score, making sure I'm getting efficient sleep, which is tough to do here.

"The lighting and everything, and what you eat and when you eat, all that stuff, it really affects you, but it's a part of the weekend, so it's massively challenging. I like it."

[Article continues below]

Hamilton excited by only one practice hit

Hamilton has arrived in Singapore off the back of a podium in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia on Sunday after finishing third behind Max Verstappen and Kimi Antonelli.

But the weekend brings another complication beyond the disrupted sleep: it is a sprint event for the first time in the history of the race, meaning just a single practice session before sprint qualifying on Friday, and then a daylight sprint race on Saturday.

It leaves no margin for error in setting up the car around the Marina Bay Street Circuit, and Hamilton says Ferrari's simulation work will need to count for more than usual.

"I honestly genuinely think we hit the ground and run pretty well in FP1 more often than not, and then, from session to session, some people close out, and some people pull away," he said.

"But I think our simulation team has done a really great job, and so I'm hoping that we start from the right place.

"It's exciting to come here to Singapore and only have one session. Everyone's in the same boat, so it could be good; it might not be good. We'll see how it goes tomorrow."

title: Oscar Piastri makes bold claim about soaring Red Bull in F1 fight with Mercedes
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri believes Red Bull has elevated itself into the same F1 bracket as Mercedes following its performances in the last two grands prix.

Verstappen finally ended his winless drought on Sunday in the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, converting pole into a comfortable victory ahead of championship leader Kimi Antonelli in his Mercedes. The second W17 of George Russell retired with a PU issue a few laps from the chequered flag.

The four-time F1 champion's triumph capped a weekend that underlined how quickly the competitive order has shifted, with Red Bull now matching Mercedes for raw pace on multiple circuit types.

In the Azerbaijan GP the previous weekend, Verstappen could only qualify eighth after a battery charging failure compromised his final Q3 lap, but he still fought through to finish second, just 0.196 seconds behind race winner Russell.

Ahead of this weekend's race in Singapore, McLaren driver Piastri said the timing and scale of Red Bull's improvement had taken him by surprise, pointing to Sepang's string of long straights as the clearest evidence yet of the team's new-found pace.

Discussing the shift in competitive order ahead of the Singapore Grand Prix, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, Piastri said: "Mercedes has been very strong the whole season, obviously. Baku, with the long straights there, it wasn't a big surprise that they were so quick.

"Considering how many straights there were in Malaysia, it was surprising they weren't faster. Whatever Red Bull put on their car in Baku clearly was big because Baku went under the radar for them with where they qualified and Max's engine problem.

"He put George under a lot of pressure at the end of the race, but I think if he had started at the front in Baku, he would have put George under a lot of pressure for the whole race.

"In Malaysia, he was definitely the quickest car and driver combination, so I definitely think the others around us are making progress.

"Us and Ferrari seem to go to and fro a little bit, but Mercedes has always been the class of the field, and I think Red Bull has kind of joined them in the last couple of weeks."

[Article continues below]

Slow street circuit corners could again undo McLaren

By contrast, McLaren arrives in Singapore having scored just 10 points across the last two rounds, with Lando Norris retiring in Baku and finishing ninth in Bahrain.

Piastri was candid about his own team's prospects around the Marina Bay Street Circuit, which is dominated by slow corners where the Woking-based squad has struggled this year.

Asked how he expected McLaren to fare this weekend, Piastri said: "We'll see what we're like.

"Slow corners have not been our strongest point this year, and street circuits neither really, so I'm not going to set my expectations super high.

"But again, being a sprint weekend, it gives a few opportunities to pull something out of the bag.

"The track surface is quite smooth; it got resurfaced a few years ago, for the most part, so maybe we'll be able to pull something forward.

"But again, it's always pretty close, so if we are ahead of the other teams, it's never going to be by much."

title: Liam Lawson delivers 'pretty fast' combo verdict on Red Bull and Racing Bulls
excerpt:
Liam Lawson believes a hybrid of the Red Bull RB22 and the Racing Bulls VCARB03 would produce a formidable package, after experiencing both machines during his unscheduled three-race recall to the senior F1 team this season.

Lawson stepped in for an injured Isack Hadjar after the summer break before returning to his regular Racing Bulls seat, giving him a rare back-to-back comparison of the two Red Bull-Ford-powered cars.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, Lawson detailed just how different the two cars feel to drive, despite sharing the same power unit.

Asked about the main differences, he replied: "Other than the power unit, pretty much everything. Honestly, it's very, very different to drive.

"So it was definitely a little bit of an adjustment to go back, but then the car is different. Just the way the steering, for example, is a bit more personal to me in my car.

"It was an adjustment for sure, but there are honestly strengths and weaknesses to both. To be honest, it's quite interesting to drive both, and you could honestly argue that if you put them together, you'd have a pretty fast race car."

[Article continues below]

Lawson - 'Singapore is a sick track'

For this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, Lawson returns to a track where he scored his first points in F1 by finishing ninth in 2023 whilst driving for AlphaTauri.

The New Zealander has conceded to being a fan of the Marina Bay Street Circuit, and is hoping Racing Bulls' recent fast starts to a weekend will lend itself to the fact that there is sprint qualifying on Friday evening rather than a second practice session.

"It's a really good track," said Lawson. "With sprint weekends, you get two shots at everything, so I'm excited.

"Recently, we've started the weekends quite strong, and then I feel like everybody else caught up, so some of that gets taken away.

"Obviously, hopefully we can start strong here, but it's just a sick track, really, really cool. It's a night race as well, so I'm excited."

title: Carlos Sainz raises health concern amid Singapore haze crisis
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz has raised health concerns about conditions in Singapore, with smoke haze from Indonesian wildfires pushing the city-state's air quality into the unhealthy bracket ahead of this weekend's grand prix.

Singapore's National Environment Agency confirmed that 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index readings across all five regions of the island crossed the unhealthy threshold in the build-up to the race, fluctuating generally between 101 and 160.

Anything above 100 on the index falls into the unhealthy category, with readings above 200 classed as very unhealthy and above 300 as hazardous.

The smoke has drifted in from agricultural and wildfire hotspots across Sumatra and Kalimantan, carried toward the region by prevailing winds and worsened by an intense weather pattern.

Hourly PM2.5 readings in parts of western and central Singapore have climbed as high as 150 micrograms per cubic metre, with brief spikes beyond that mark.

The situation is being monitored by F1, as to be expected. Despite the conditions, there are no concerns, with on-track running not anticipated to be interrupted.

[Article continues below]

Sainz - 'A funny sport anyway'

Sainz said he had been following the situation closely.

"I've read a bit about it. It doesn't feel like the healthiest place to be breathing right now, given the amount of pollution from the fires in Indonesia," the Williams driver said.

"In these cases, we always go by what the authorities say, and if the authorities say it's good to do sport outside, like we are doing, which I'm not sure they are saying that..."

Told that the official directive is to limit outdoor activity, the Spaniard continued: "You know, it's a funny sport anyway.

"When we are racing, we are breathing the fuel burn of the car in front. We've done that since we were 11, 12 years old.

"So it's debatable whether it's a healthy or unhealthy sport, but we do it; we like it. It smells great. At least I love the smell of fuel.

"The haze is a different matter, obviously, but we need to go by what the authorities say."

title: Fred Vasseur handed 'welcome respite' after dazzling Lewis Hamilton display
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton drove to an unlikely podium last time out in Malaysia after an early-race tyre disaster.

Former F1 driver David Coulthard believes Lewis Hamilton's result at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was a “welcome respite” for Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur.

For several weeks, there has been mounting scrutiny on Vasseur's shoulders, with increased speculation that he could be heading for the exit door at the Maranello-based squad.

The rumours kicked up another notch when Christian Horner declared he would accept a non-shareholding role at Ferrari if he was offered the team boss role.

Ferrari moved to squash the speculation ahead of the race event in Sepang by declaring it was backing Vasseur, who has been in the role for almost four years.

After opting to start the race on the wrong tyre in varying weather conditions, both Hamilton and team-mate Charles Leclerc plummeted down the order. However, both recovered to end the race in third and fourth, respectively.

Coulthard has theorised that this will ease the pressure on Vasseur's shoulders.

"Hamilton's result shows that it's not over until it's over," Coulthard told the Up to Speed podcast.

"There were a bunch of circumstances that brought him back into it, but if you lost your head and then threw in the towel, he would never have been able to achieve that.

"It's probably a welcome respite for Fred from the criticisms that he's had."

[Article continues below]

Ferrari 'finding their form'

Hamilton has endured a largely positive campaign with Ferrari, getting a breakthrough win in Barcelona and adding multiple podiums to his list of successes.

While hopes of an eighth title have been all but extinguished, Coulthard stated it has been a campaign for him to be proud of.

"Lewis, after qualifying [in Malaysia], was giddy with excitement about how good the car was and that he had qualified second," he said.

"He was complimentary about the procedures within the garage and how they went about getting him out on the track in the right space.

"So it feels like out of some disappointments this year, they're finding their form.

"It also shows again that Lewis has consistently just got that little edge over Charles, which wasn't the case in year one.

"He seems to have found a comfort and a zone there, so it'll be interesting to watch that intra-team battle."

title: F1 drivers handed overwhelming support over thorny track design topic
excerpt:
F1 drivers have been handed unequivocal support when it comes to ensuring they are heard on future track design.

A RacingNews365 poll showed that fans are firmly on the side of the drivers when it comes to circuit design, with 94.5 per cent agreeing that those behind the wheel know best what makes for good overtaking.

Just 3.6 per cent of respondents took the opposite view, that drivers should simply race what they are given and keep their opinions to themselves. The remainder said they did not know.

The poll came following renewed debate over circuit layouts after the inaugural Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring hybrid circuit, which drew sharp criticism from multiple drivers for offering few realistic passing opportunities.

Alexander Albon was among the most vocal advocates for change, arguing that modern permanent circuits with camber, elevation changes and varied corner angles create pockets of clean air that street tracks often lack.

Lewis Hamilton voiced similar frustration after the Madring weekend, questioning the credentials of those behind recent track designs.

"They're making some of these tracks where you just cannot overtake, and it's frustrating," the Ferrari driver said. "Don't know who's designing them... like, anyone else here wanna design a track?

"I'm pretty certain there are lots of people who would be able to do a better job than some of the ones we've got come up."

George Russell echoed the call for structural change, insisting: "They need to make a change because every track needs to have an overtaking opportunity after a bit of a straight."

title: George Russell confirms double punishment blow after agonising Mercedes failure
excerpt:
George Russell has confirmed he will take a second grid penalty before the end of the season, on top of the one he faces this weekend at the Singapore Grand Prix, after his Mercedes engine failed in the closing stages in Sepang.

Russell retired with a power unit failure in the closing laps of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, ending a race in which teammate Kimi Antonelli finished second.

The unit that failed is now being replaced, triggering a grid penalty at Marina Bay, but Russell has revealed that a further change, and another penalty, is now unavoidable later in the campaign.

Speaking to select media including RacingNews365 on Singapore media day, Russell explained that the engine which failed was not actually overdue for retirement.

Asked whether the failure was caused by the power unit being used for too long, the Briton was unequivocal.

"No, the engine wasn't stretched too long," said Russell. "It was the sixth race of the engine, and obviously you have four engines a year, six races per engine when you split it up.

"We actually put that engine in on Sunday in Budapest, so it was actually the sixth race, but minus qualifying and the practice sessions of Budapest."

George Russell reveals Mercedes' engine change delay hope

Russell said Mercedes had been trying to delay a penalty until it could fit an upgraded unit built under the FIA's Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities mechanism, which the Brackley-based squad qualified for after its engine trailed Red Bull's on the official performance index.

"We were waiting to take the engine penalty with the ADUO update, but obviously, unfortunately, we've had to take it here [in Singapore]," added Russell.

"But with seven races remaining, that's longer than the engines are designed for. Unfortunately, it means I'll be taking another penalty at some point between the next race and the end of the season, so yeah, feels a little bit like one thing after another right now.

"But that's just how the cookie crumbles."

title: Max Verstappen issues clear-cut stance over 'stupid' driver aid
excerpt:
Max Verstappen will not be making use of this contraption available to him in Singapore this weekend.

Max Verstappen has insisted he will not use the cooling vest on offer this weekend at the Singapore Grand Prix due to the “stupid” cables that cause limitations.

With a heat hazard declared by the FIA in Singapore, drivers now have the option to use the cooling vest, designed to offer relief in extreme conditions.

The concept originated after several drivers fell ill after the 2023 Qatar Grand Prix.

But Verstappen has insisted that he will not be making use of it in Singapore, despite it often being the toughest physical challenge the drivers will face all year.

“For me, it's not needed,” Verstappen told media including RacingNews365. “Yes, it's hot, but it's not a sauna.

“And with the cooling vest, you have these stupid cables in your car, so you're just limiting your movement as well.

“I don't need it. Even if it would work for one and a half hours, cool. But I don't need it.

“It doesn't work anyway for one and a half hours. I've never [heard], in any category, that it has worked for one and a half hours.”

Verstappen has 'unfinished business' in Singapore

Verstappen enters the Singapore race weekend having bagged his first win of the season last time out in Malaysia.

Curiously, despite his vast success throughout his F1 career, he has not yet stood on the top step of the podium at the Marina Bay Circuit.

It is a shortcoming the four-time champion is seeking to rectify this weekend.

“In the last few years we've always been bad at low speed, low speed and just kerbing, bumps,” Verstappen said.

“This car is probably more competitive in low speed, but we still struggle on bumps and kerbs.

“I have unfinished business when you have not won the race. Naturally, every year I come back and I'm trying to win it.

“But it also needs to be realistic. But I always try every single year, and I hope that we can be a little bit more competitive this year.”

title: Lewis Hamilton bemoans FIA and young F1 drivers over wet-weather caution
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton feels F1's current wet-weather approach is overly cautious, pointing the finger at both FIA race control and the younger generation of drivers.

Hamilton finished third in Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, climbing from 18th early on after starting on slicks to the podium behind race winner Max Verstappen and Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli.

Heavy rain before the race began triggered a 40-minute delay. The event eventually commenced behind the safety car for what was meant to be two formation laps, and a possible standing start.

That did not materialise, however, due to a software 'bug that infected several systems, including that of Hamilton in his Ferrari. He had to stop on track, and reboot the SF-26 to get going again.

Hamilton, who started that race on the front row alongside polesitter Verstappen, said he had been relishing the prospect of wheel-to-wheel battles in the rain, only to see the opportunity disappear.

"I was looking forward to a wet race," said Hamilton, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365. "When it started raining, I was like, 'Oh yeah, this is going to be fun.

"We did the laps to the grid, and there was obviously a lot of spray, and then with all the delay and everything like that, ultimately I didn't get to have that battle that I wanted to have with Max, which I was excited about, and Kimi."

[Article continues below]

The seven-time F1 champion, who has spoken previously about his affection for driving in treacherous conditions, drew a direct comparison with his early career, when Bridgestone's rain tyres were developed through far greater on-track mileage than today's Pirelli compounds.

"Wet weather races aren't the same as we used to have," Hamilton said. "I've had great races in the rain, like 2008 [his British GP victory]. Ultimately, we had more testing back then.

"We had better tyres for the rain because we were able to...I guess they were developed more with Bridgestone back in the day.

"And I love racing in the rain, personally."

Taking umbrage with some of the decisions that are made when it comes to racing in the wet, Hamilton added: "I do think the guys running the show [in FIA race control] are more and more and more cautious, but then again, the young drivers coming in are more and more cautious.

"Us old-school drivers are like, 'Let's get racing', and the youngsters are like, 'Let's not race'.

"So they [FIA race control] are getting two different bits of information, and they are super cautious as well.

"Whereas I'm like, 'Let's get going' under extreme conditions, because that's where we really get to test ourselves.

"Is it more risky? Absolutely. When I was on the slick tyre [in Malaysia], it was the trickiest conditions. It's wet, and I'm on slicks. But I love that challenge, and that's what racing is, where you have to drive by the seat of your pants.

"That's really where you can make the difference, and ultimately, that is where I did make the difference at the end of the day."

title: Why F1 will make bizarre Singapore Grand Prix history this weekend
excerpt:
Formula 1 will make history at Marina Bay this weekend when Saturday's Sprint race becomes the first competitive session in Singapore Grand Prix history to be held in daylight rather than under floodlights.

Every grand prix held in Singapore since the event's debut in 2008 has taken place at night, with Marina Bay serving as F1's first-ever night race.

That remains the case for this weekend's main grand prix, which is still scheduled for its traditional evening slot.

But the sprint, set for 17:00 local time on Saturday, will run in daylight before darkness falls for qualifying later that evening.

The scheduling quirk stems from the need for a mandatory four-hour buffer between the start of the sprint and the night qualifying session that follows, while also allowing support categories to run their own events in Marina Bay's evening prime-time slot.

Lando Norris addresses unusual Singapore GP Sprint

Lando Norris does not expect the unusual timing to have much bearing on performance, telling select media, including RacingNews365, that Singapore's climate stays largely consistent whatever the hour.

"I don't think it changes too much, honestly, because it's not like it gets a lot colder or warmer depending on the time," said the McLaren driver.

"It's just always pretty hot here. So here, not so much [of a difference]. I think in other places, Bahrain, for example, it can be quite the opposite.

"During the day, it's horrible in terms of the effect the temperature has, and in the evenings, the track gets a lot quicker, the car works worse, all of those things. So there's a big effect. Here, I think it's quite a bit smaller, and it's just more consistent."

"So, honestly, I'm going to go with I don't think there's too much of a difference between it. It's just visually things look different, but that's really the main thing."

Norris's comments echo the technical picture around Marina Bay's unusual conditions. Track temperatures at the street circuit are driven far more by the presence or absence of direct sunlight than by swings in the ambient air, which stays roughly stable between day and night due to Singapore's near-equatorial location.

That is markedly different to a venue like Bahrain, where desert night races produce a sharp drop in air temperature once the sun sets, fundamentally altering tyre behaviour and track grip.

Teams are expected to treat Saturday's daytime sprint running with some caution when it comes to setup relevance, given that hotter asphalt and a dirtier track surface in sunlight typically behave differently to the cooler, more rubbered-in conditions under the floodlights come qualifying and the race itself.

title: Ferrari release 'statement' after Lewis Hamilton-Charles Leclerc social media chaos
excerpt:
Ferrari has released a “statement” after its social media was taken over by Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc on Thursday in Singapore.

For a handful of hours, Hamilton and Leclerc gained access to the social media accounts, posting several images and videos on Instagram and X.

While it included normal behind-the-scenes access to Ferrari's motorhome, both drivers took time to mess with camera filters, while also changing the team's profile picture to a selfie image, commenting on other drivers' posts and engaging with fans.

It prompted Ferrari to release a light-hearted message, addressing the takeover.

“Scuderia Ferrari HP confirms that, over the past two hours, two individuals within the organisation gained unauthorised control of our social media channels,” it said.

“During this period, a series of highly questionable editorial decisions were made, including changes to our profile picture and the publication of content that did not undergo our standard approval procedures.

“We can confirm that the two suspects have been identified and the situation has now been contained. Full control of our accounts has been restored.

“We thank our fans for their understanding during this unprecedented incident.”
